result:
The question assumes "more agents always give better results", and that isn't true. So the answer isn't five or ten. For your assistant, the answer is probably one agent.

Splitting work across agents has a real price. Anthropic's engineering team reports that a single agent uses about 4× the tokens of a plain chat, and a multi-agent system about 15×. Their multi-agent setup did beat a single agent on their research tasks. Those tasks were broad ones, where many independent directions can be searched at the same time. Your sponsor gave you a small model budget, so a 15× cost is a big deal.

The tasks in your assistant don't fit that pattern:

- Answering a question from a manual means finding one page and reading it.
- Checking the calendar and booking a slot are short steps that depend on each other. Each step needs the result of the one before it.

Splitting those across several agents adds cost and hand-off mistakes, and it buys little. It's tempting because "more agents" sounds more capable.

A better order of work:
1. Start with one agent that has three well-described tools: manual search, calendar check and booking.
2. Make any step that is always the same a fixed workflow, not an agent decision.
3. Add a second agent only if you can name the problem it solves, such as a context so crowded that quality drops.

At your design review, "we measured a problem and split because of it" is a much stronger argument than "ten is more than five."

Quick check: your assistant gets "Is the laser cutter free Thursday at 3, and can I use it with my training?". Which parts would you run in parallel, and which must wait for another step's result?

Source: [Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). I only read a short excerpt of the page. The 4× and 15× figures and the benefit on broad research tasks come from that excerpt.

I can write a lesson on workflows versus agents and when multi-agent pays off if you want one.
